The natural language uses 'if and only if' which implies logical equivalence (biconditional), meaning P is true exactly when (not Q) is true, which also includes the case where both P and (not Q) are false. Thus, (P ⊕ ¬Q) is not equivalent to (P ↔ ¬Q). The closest is (P ↔ ¬Q) which means (P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ Q). The exclusive OR P ⊕ Q means (P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ (¬ P ∧ Q). Therefore, (P ⊕ ¬Q) corresponds to 'x is a public figure or x holds a prestigious award, but not both'. The NL 'if and only if' requires biconditional (↔).
